title: A $10 Sensor Uses Light to Test Things Like a Lab
summary:
Scientists at the University of Cambridge in England have built a tiny light sensor that costs about $10. It can measure things as well as big lab machines.

The sensor is a spectrometer. It studies light that touches an object. Different materials change light in different ways, so the light shows what something is made of.

Small spectrometers are usually not very accurate. The Cambridge team used a clever math idea to make theirs work better. It is just a few centimeters wide and works in less than a second.

In tests, it correctly named plastics, medicines, coffee, flour and tea every time. It also measured things in the body, like skin moisture and blood sugar, in lab conditions.

One day, it might help people check blood sugar without needles. But the scientists say more testing is needed first. The sensor also worked in very cold and very hot temperatures.
why_it_matters: Small, cheap sensors could one day help people check their health with something as simple as a watch.
